Varicella (chickenpox) is a common acute infectious disease. It is caused by varicella-zoster virus (VZV), which is a DNA virus that is a member of the herpes virus group. After the primary infection, VZV stays in the body (in the sensory nerve ganglia) as a latent infection. Primary infection with VZV leads to varicella. Reactivation of latent infection causes herpes zoster (shingles). The average incubation period for varicella is 14 – 16 days after exposure to a varicella or a herpes zoster rash, with a range of 10 to 21 days. Varicella is very infectious. The infection can be spread from individual to individual by direct contact, from vesicular liquid of skin sores of intense varicella or zoster, and potentially through tainted respiratory discharges that likewise might be aerosolized. An individual with varicella is infectious starting 2 to 6 days before rash beginning until all the chickenpox sores have crusted. Inoculated individuals may create injuries that don't heal. The maximum infectivity period is reported to be 6 days before formation of vesicle. These individuals are viewed as infectious until no new injuries have showed up for 24 hours. It takes from 10 to 21 days after presentation to the infection for somebody to create varicella. In view of investigations of transmission among family individuals, about 90% of powerless close contacts will get varicella after presentation to an individual with illness.

All the movements characteristic of the tonic phase will occur at the same time and will continue for up to 30 seconds before the seizure proceeds into the clonic phase. Convulsive movements affect all four limbs and most facial muscles. The limbs abduct and extend repeatedly for up to 1 minute. Breathing may get impaired, and as the muscles involving breathing might have contracted, air will be expelled, generating an abnormal noise. As the patient is unresponsive, chances of tongue bite, collapsing of tongue backward may occur which in turn learn to suffocation. Nursing responsibilities include:
    • Arrest convulsion part
    • Maintenance of patent airway, breathing and circulation
    • Oxygen administration at the rate 8 – 10 L/Min
    • Terminate pregnancy

    • Prevention of complication

  • Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) is the agent most commonly used for treatment of eclampsia and prophylaxis of eclampsia in patients with severe pre-eclampsia. MgSO4 is administered intramuscular or intravenous routes. If it is given as intramuscular then dosage is 4 g intravenous loading dose, immediately followed by 10 g intramuscularly and then by 5 g intramuscularly every 4 hours in alternating buttocks. If it’s given intravenously the dosage will be a 4 g dose, followed by a maintenance infusion of 1 to 2 g/h by controlled infusion pump. Hence the administration of MgSO4 is priority among the list.

• Projection is one of the most common ego defense mechanism, which comes under psychotic defense mechanism in which a person portrays his own unacceptable thoughts, desires, and feelings on to someone else. The individual attributes his own undesirable and uncomfortable traits on to others thereby trying to compromise with the stressful situation.
  • For example: A student attributing the reason for failing in an exam as teacher’s partiality or fever the day before exam. Clinical illustration examples are persecutory delusions and hallucinations.
  • Regression is also a psychotic defense mechanism, which is characterized by going back to modes of psychological functioning that are features of childhood behavior. It is the defense mechanism in which one returns to a less mature behavior and responsibility to face frustration. In simpler terms, an adult engaging in childlike behavior (e.g. nail biting) during stress.
  • Dissociation: Normal mental functioning is propagated by coordinated acts of identity, memory and consciousness, sometimes in stressful situations these three splits apart from the rest of personality and the resulting state of defense is called dissociation. • Established enzyme biomarkers of myocardial infarction are Troponin T, Troponin I, myocardial fraction of CK and myoglobin. Troponins are released into the circulation 6 – 8 hours after myocardial injury, peak at 12 – 24 hour and remain elevated for 7 – 10 days. Myoglobulin (MYO) is a small cytoplasmic oxygen-binding protein found in the skeletal as well as the cardiac muscle. It is released extremely early into the serum, 1 hour after the onset of myocardial injury, peaks at 4 – 12 hour and returns to baseline values immediately. • Potassium is the electrolyte that is most affected in DKA. Acidosis causes hydrogen ions to move from the extracellular fluid into the intracellular space.
  • Hydrogen movement into the cell promotes movement of potassium out of the cell into the extracellular compartment (including the intravascular space). Severe intracellular potassium depletion follows. Potassium levels can fluctuate severely during the treatment of DKA, because insulin decreases potassium levels in the blood by redistributing it into cells  via increased sodium-potassium pump activity.
  • A large part of the shifted extracellular potassium would have been lost in urine because of osmotic diuresis. Hypokalemia  (low blood potassium concentration) often follows treatment. This increases the risk of  dangerous irregularities in the heart rate. Therefore, continuous observation of the heart rate is recommended,  as well as repeated measurement of the potassium levels and addition of potassium to the intravenous fluids once levels fall below 5.3  mmol/L.
  • If potassium levels fall below 3.3 mmol/L, insulin administration may need to be interrupted to allow correction of the hypokalemia.
  • Calcium, Magnesium and Sodium is not needed to be replaced in diabetic ketoacidosis

Prothrombin time (PT) is a blood test that analyzes the time that blood takes to clot. A Prothrombin time test is usually performed to check bleeding problems. PT is also used to evaluate whether anticoagulant medications which are given to prevent coagulation for patients with arteriosclerosis and associated disorders are working or not. A PT test may also be called an INR test. INR is the short form of international normalized ratio. • Autoclaving is a very commonly used sterilization method which uses high pressure steam, this concept is based on the theory that boiling point of water rises under pressure. For getting effective results the temperature should reach at 121°C for 30 minutes under 15 psi of pressure. The autoclave is an equipment, which is used to remove microorganisms (Virus, Bacteria, fungus, etc.) and spores using high pressure and high temperature steam sterilization.
  • Types of Autoclaves
    • Heat autoclaves: The most common source for autoclaving is heating. Here the autoclaves should maintain a temperature of at least 246 degrees for half an hour. Both dry heat or steam heat are used. For steam-heat autoclaves, heated water vapors are used. Dry heat autoclaves are used for moisture-sensitive surgical products or instruments.
    • Gas autoclaves: Gas autoclaves use a vapor solution to sterilize its contents. Formaldehyde gas and ethylene oxide are the sterilizing agents used in gas autoclaves. They consume lesser heat and take lesser time to complete the cycle.
    • Ultraviolet autoclaves: They produce UV light that kills the unwanted disease-causing organisms.
    • Cold sterilization autoclaves: They use a cold sterilization liquid to sterilize the contents.
    • Laboratory autoclaves: They are used for general lab work, component and stability testing, core hardening, drying glassware and sterilizing.
    • Stove top autoclaves: In such autoclaves, the tools should always be separated to allow the steam to penetrate the load evenly. It is the simplest autoclave.

• Sodium nitroprusside: An extremely elevated level of arterial blood pressure is termed as malignant hypertension. In most of the cases it leads to organ failure and often death. This condition is considered as hypertensive emergency. The development of this situation is often rapid, the blood pressure level will reach around 180/120 mm Hg or above. Intravenous sodium nitroprusside is the drug of choice to treat malignant hypertension. The dosage is 0.3 to 0.5 mcg/kg/minute to a maximum dosage of 10 mcg/kg/minute. Fenoldopam and Labetalol are other alternative drugs. The brand name sodium nitorprusside is Nitropress. Sodium Nitroprusside is nitrate group of drugs. Mechanism of action: Nitric oxide produced due to this drug act as a vasodilator, causing the muscles around the blood vessels to relax. Onset of action is immediate, and its effects last up to ten minutes. Since it is short acting drug, it is drug of choice for malignant hypertension when compared with other options listed. Even though the nitroglycerin is also nitrate group, the reach of target level was quick in sodium nitroprusside when compared to nitroglycerin.
  • Atenolol is a beta blocker commonly used to treat hypertension but not indicated in malignant hypertension.
  • Amlodipine is a long-acting calcium-channel blocker usually indicated in primary hypertension, the dosage usually starts at 2.5–5 mg single oral dose, but not suggested for treating malignant hypertension.
  • Nitroglycerine is a nitrate group of drug often used to treat angina pectoris associated with coronary artery disease.
